questions.text: Why does this lesson store access tokens under both issuer and resource rather than resource alone?

options.A: To let all resources share a token whenever the user is the same.
options.B: To replace server-side audience validation with a client cache key.
options.C: To allow an issuer’s refresh token to enroll clients at another issuer.
options.D: To keep tokens tied to the authorization server and intended protected service.

questions.explanation: Issuer and resource identify who issued the token and where it is intended to be used. Their binding prevents cross-issuer or cross-resource token confusion.

questions.text: The client holds a token for the MCP notes service, which must call a downstream API. How should it authenticate to that downstream API?

options.A: Forward the notes-service token because the user already consented.
options.B: Obtain a separate token for the downstream audience or use explicit token exchange.
options.C: Put the notes-service token in the downstream URL for routing.
options.D: Change the token’s audience field locally before forwarding it.

questions.explanation: A token intended for the MCP resource must not be passed through to a different audience. Use an appropriately issued downstream credential.

questions.text: In Client.authorize, the expected issuer is "https://auth.example.com", but response["iss"] is "https://auth.example.com/". What happens before auth.exchange is called?

options.A: The client strips the trailing slash and exchanges the code.
options.B: The client stores the token under both issuer spellings.
options.C: The exact comparison fails and raises ValueError.
options.D: The client ignores iss because the response contains a code.

questions.explanation: The code compares the issuer strings exactly and raises on mismatch before exchanging the authorization code.
